It has been revealed that most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate initiative must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:.

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

It has been revealed that before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

Industry observers note that without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

Key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

You have decades of retirement ahead during which a lawsuit, car accident judgment, or liability claim could threaten the wealth you worked so hard to build.

Industry observers note that for FIRE households pursuing charitable giving, a donor-advised fund (DAF) allows you to front-load charitable deductions in high-income years (or Roth conversion years), reduce your taxable estate, and distribute grants to charities over time. A DAF contribution is irrevocable and immediately reduces your estate while giving you advisory control over future grants.

It has been revealed that do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate plan. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

In a recent development, for most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

Yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

According to recent reports, review your estate proposal every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a newly introduced state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more key than for conventional retirees.

According to recent reports, estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate blueprint: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

Breaking: Maren Hassinger Won’t Be Weighed Down

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Maren Hassinger’s retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) has a radiant warmth about it—surprisingly so, given that it’s a show made mostly of gray metal sculptures whose edges could prick you raw.
  • According to recent reports, rejected in college from Bennington’s dance department in the 1960s, Hassinger was pushed toward sculpture by a teacher who noticed her gift.
  • Sources indicate that in graduate school, at UCLA, Hassinger was rerouted once again after finding the sculpture program to be a boys’ club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maren Hassinger’s retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) has a radiant warmth about it—surprisingly so, given that it’s a show made mostly of gray metal sculptures whose edges could prick you raw. This warmth owes a lot to the photographs, printed mural-sized and filling vitrines, taken by her long-term collaborator Adam Avila. Scattered throughout, they show Hassinger dancing, beaming, and/or hamming it up for the camera, often mirroring her sculpture’s forms with her body. But it owes, too, to the ways she rose to meet her career’s surprising twists and turns. Related Articles ARTnews Awards 2026 Lifetime Achievement: Maren Hassinger Maren Hassinger to Receive Her Largest Retrospective to Date Next Year.

According to recent reports, rejected in college from Bennington’s dance department in the 1960s, Hassinger was pushed toward sculpture by a teacher who noticed her gift. “My love of motion,” she says in the catalog, carried her from one to the other. Clement Greenberg was a guest at her senior thesis critique: He had “the gift of gab, but was a bit of a bully” she remembers with accurate alliterations. He would not be her last mean man.

Sources indicate that in graduate school, at UCLA, Hassinger was rerouted once again after finding the sculpture program to be a boys’ club. As she remembers it, not one single woman was enrolled. So she found a home in fiber, a typical tale, and made it work: “Truthfully,” she admits in the catalog, “I was just trying to get a degree so I could teach and make art.” But she found herself too impatient for the loom and uninterested in making fabric. So she gathered fibers out in the world, chancing upon a weighty rope in a shipyard. It was made of blonde hemp but discolored by oil. Playing around, she eventually unraveled some of its strands before tying segments into a series of loose, giant macrame knots that greet visitors to BAMPFA, where they lie on the ground as if waiting to be pulled tight.

Hassinger would marry craft techniques with industrial materials henceforth—a revealing portrait of women’s changing work in her time. She became such a regular at one LA wire shop that they featured her on the cover of their trade magazine. Soon, she was incorporating elevator cables—effectively wire ropes, their cords twisted together—into what would become her best known works. Leaning (1980) sees cables with frayed ends bundled in some two dozen bouquets. Only the central arrangement has a flat bottom and sits sturdily; the rest are free to lean.

Fiber meets metal in River, a 2,000-pound rope-chain Hassinger made as an ambitious graduate student in 1972. But where was a student to store such a behemoth? Recognition would not come until much later—as the title of her work Wallflower series (1975) attests—so she let River go, then finally remade it in 2011 for a Studio Museum acquisition. (Good thing she had so many photographs). A few other works at BAMPFA are recreations, too, but after school, she mainly made sculptures that could be coiled up and made compact: a resourceful response to the realities of real estate.

To see Hassinger’s work is to think about the act of making it. It shows you: Knots are blown up big so that you can see each twist and turn. Her titles are often verbs, as with Whirling (1978), Walking (1978), and Leaning (1980). “When she talks about the work, she moves” explained Margot Norton, who co-curated the show with Anthony Graham.

In a recent development, hassinger met the obstacles that came her way, as a Black woman born in 1947, with poetry and practicality in equal measure. Of her turn to newspaper, which she twisted and knotted for a cascading 2008 installation, she explains that the material “is very handy and cheap [laughs].” But it also must have been cathartic to rip the headlines into strips. Her resourcefulness and resilience define the show, which sees her rethink sculpture without storage, fiber without fabric, choreography without corporeality.

Industry observers note that hassinger hardly did it alone. “Working alone is so antisocial” as she quips in the catalog. When Senga Nengudi first saw Hassinger’s work in 1975, she was thrilled to see another Black woman working with sculpture and performance, then looked her up. They became fast friends. With David Hammons, Nengudi then suggested that Linda Goode-Bryant show Hassinger at her gallery, Just Above Midtown (JAM). That show’s main work, Beach (1980), is installed at BAMPFA, too.

When Hassinger’s cohort of Black LA artists—known as Studio Z—lacked opportunities, they invented their own, as when Hassinger, Nengudi, Ulysses Jenkins, and others performed at the 1982 opening of “Afro-American Abstractions.” They had neither hung work on the walls nor been included in the checklist, but they did call up the Los Angeles Municipal Art Gallery to accept a nonexistent invitation: “We are so thrilled to be doing the opening performance!” they informed whoever answered the phone.

In the 1990s, Hassinger found herself without a studio. Starved for space, she turned to video. Birthright (2005) is nothing like her sculptures, but it will forever change how you see them. Onscreen, the artist interviews her uncle about her family tree. She learns that her grandmother, Puddin, had been the product both of incest and an interracial affair. Puddin’s parents hadn’t known that they were nephew and aunt, because Puddin’s father was born out of wedlock to his lover’s father who had a secret Native mistress.

Once the affair was discovered, Puddin was given away to a plantation caretaker who had been enslaved, and her father was lynched by a white mob. Puddin’s son—Hassinger’s dad—never talked about any of this: He was abandoned too by Puddin, then struggled to relate to women, cutting Hassinger out of the will and passing down patterns. “My legacy was to feel unloved,” the artist concludes in the video. But then the show keeps going.

Right next to Birthright, the curators installed Love (2008/2026), and it is here—halfway through the retrospective—that galleries of gray give way to hot pink. Plastic shopping bags filled with human breath and love notes cover the walls. Her lightness beams off the building, but look closely and you’ll find a sense of play throughout the show.

Sources indicate that thinking about familial lineages, Hassinger’s knots and ropes start to feel like umbilical cords severed and frayed. History is hefty, but it never weighs the work down in any sense of the word. “I always felt so good when I danced,” the artist explains, “lighter, faster.” It is easy to imagine her dancing in her studio while walking around BAMPFA, where one gets a sense of heaviness made to look light. Untitled (1972/2020) sees ropes with looped ends, noose-like, but instead of being tied into knots, strands are undone and then woven back together seamlessly. In the galleries, the ropes dangle gracefully from the ceiling and weigh heavy on the floor.

Hassinger is an artist who sees things soberly as they are and imaginatively as they might be—a gift that enables her to turn junkyard findings into elegant arrays and litter into love.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, now in its fourth year, DGW was launched in 2023 by the city’s commercial galleries to raise the profile of its contemporary art scene.
  • According to recent reports, while the artists I spoke to described the BIA as a major boost to their working lives, I found little evidence that it has fundamentally changed Dublin’s contemporary art scene.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that life was pretty rosy for the 2,000 Irish artists who landed a spot on Ireland’s Basic Income for the Arts (BIA) pilot scheme. For three years, from 2022 to 2025, €325 arrived in their bank accounts every week. The money was intended to provide a dependable income, reduce the need to take on unrelated jobs to cover living costs, and give artists more time to concentrate on making art. Judging by the recipients I spoke earlier this month at Dublin Gallery Weekend (DGW), the pilot was a success. And since the BIA was made permanent in February, thousands more artists are hoping to reap the rewards.“Basic Income for the Arts is a game changer, and now it is here to stay,” Ireland’s minister for culture, communications, and sport, Patrick O’Donovan, mentioned in February. Related Articles Ireland's Museum Staffers Struggle with Precarious Contracts and Toxic Environments National Museum of Ireland Employee Charged in Alleged Car Bomb Plot.

In a recent development, now in its fourth year, DGW was launched in 2023 by the city’s commercial galleries to raise the profile of its contemporary art scene. Organized by the Contemporary Art Gallery Association (CAGA), this year’s four-day program brought together galleries and cultural institutions for exhibitions, talks, screenings, and performances. A major addition was the inaugural Francis Bacon Awards for Irish Visual Arts, a €40,000 prize fund supported by Château La Coste. Painter Patrick Graham received the €25,000 Lifetime Achievement Award, while Belfast-born artist Cathy Wilkes took the €15,000 Mid-Career prize. Both will stage solo exhibitions at Château La Coste in Provence, France.

According to recent reports, while the artists I spoke to described the BIA as a major boost to their working lives, I found little evidence that it has fundamentally changed Dublin’s contemporary art scene. None of the dealers, curators, or museum directors I spoke to suggested that its impact had been felt on a wider scale across the city’s galleries or commercial market.

Applications for the BIA’s newly introduced three-year round opened in May, with previous recipients eligible to reapply for one of the 2,000 available places. Around 10,000 artists applied, making competition fierce for a program to which the Irish government has committed €18 million.

Industry observers note that “Over the course of the scheme, my practice flourished,” Dublin-based artist Gearóid O’Dea, who was selected for the pilot, told ARTnews. The funding allowed him to curate an exhibition based on Samuel Beckett’s work that travelled to Berlin, and collaborate with four other artists through the Glue Factory collective. He stated the financial support made it possible to bring artists together and exhibit internationally without constantly having to find other jobs to make ends meet.

Sources indicate that cork-born Elinor O’Donovan, who is now studying for a master’s degree in Gothenburg, Sweden, also received the pilot payment. She told ARTnews that “it completely transformed my ability to work as an artist.”.

Before joining the scheme, O’Donovan worked part-time as a receptionist alongside her artistic practice. The weekly payment allowed her to give up the job and concentrate on making art full-time. “Knowing the money was coming for three years was a big relief,” she noted. “My psychological wellbeing improved because there was security.”.

Lauren, another former recipient who is now based in London, mentioned the payment arrived at a pivotal moment in her career. Having just completed her undergraduate degree, she had secured a graduate residency at the Royal Hibernian Academy in Dublin, where she was given a studio and access to painting classes. The BIA helped her develop her practice and take up further opportunities, including residencies and exhibitions. She has since secured funding to continue her studies in London. “There’s kind of nothing I haven’t done in the last four or five years that hasn’t, in some way, been impacted by my experience with the basic income,” she told ARTnews.

According to recent reports, despite the BIA’s unprecedented support for artists, not everyone is waxing lyrical about it, including some who benefited from the original pilot. Tadhg Ó Cuirrín, a visual artist who received the payment and works with the artists’ trade union Praxis, believes the government has missed an opportunity to build on its success. More than 10,000 artists applied for the new round, yet the number of places remains unchanged at 2,000. Recipients will also be limited to three years of support in every six-year period.

“It feels less like a base income per se and more like a kind of a multi-annual grant chosen by lottery,” he told ARTnews.

Although the program is now permanent, individual artists are not guaranteed support beyond three years. Artists must meet the scheme’s eligibility criteria, after which places are allocated through a lottery, with selection also taking demographic representation into account. Ó Cuirrín argued that the three-years-on, three-years-off model reinstates the financial insecurity BIA was designed to address. Artists risk losing their income just as their practices are beginning to flourish.

It has been revealed that O’Dea has reapplied for the newly introduced round but is still waiting to hear if he’s been selected. He said the prospect of losing the regular income has brought financial anxiety back into his life.

Sources indicate that the transition has also caused difficulties for artists who relied on other forms of state support. Michaële Cutaya, a spokesperson for Praxis, previously told The Art Newspaper that some former recipients have had to return to other work to cover their living costs. “If you have to then take on a different kind of job, it’s really disruptive,” she mentioned.

Noel Kelly, chief executive of Visual Artists Ireland, said he welcomes the permanent scheme, but pointed to practical problems. BIA payments can affect artists receiving means-tested benefits, including disability allowance, while some applicants’ immigration status may prevent them from registering as self-employed, a requirement for participation.

Sources indicate that kelly also cautioned against judging the program solely on its financial return. An independent evaluation estimated that every euro invested generated €1.39 in social and economic benefits, taking into account factors including improved wellbeing. Kelly remarked that calculation misses much of what artists contribute to society.

It has been revealed that “I hate that argument,” he told ARTnews. “It allows us to participate one in the local community, two in the local economy, three in the local creative ecology.”.

Recent findings suggest that the impact of the BIA on Ireland’s commercial art market is harder to measure. John Daly, director of Hillsboro Fine Art and chair of the Contemporary Art Gallery Association, told ARTnews that the country’s galleries continue to operate with a relatively small pool of collectors. “Success actually is survival,” he noted. Daly argued the Irish art scene needs to attract younger collectors and encourage greater corporate support. Despite the presence of major international technology companies like Google in Dublin, he said corporate collecting remains limited, with companies tending to support arts initiatives such as murals and workshops. “It should be a huge opportunity, given the presence of all these multinationals, but not yet.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.

UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their “cutting-edge” environmental prototypes.

Described as the “world’s first seaweed-based single-use earplug”, SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.

According to SearoSoft, the soft, mouldable earplugs are made without microplastics or chemicals and designed to hydrate the ear canal, unlike plastic-based products, which can be drying.

Once discarded, they are biodegradable in water or soil after 30 days. As seaweed is a regenerative crop, SearoSoft explained that there is no need for land, freshwater or fertilisers, making the process simple and more sustainable.

Industry observers note that among the other prototypes is a building material project by Sussex-based Local Works Studio. The initiative, named Ferment, will repurpose agricultural waste into an insulating material fit for retrofitting buildings.

Local Works Studio aims to develop an accessible product for farms via what it calls a “harvest-to-house system”, where farmers can produce the insulation themselves using their existing infrastructure, skills and machinery.

Bristol-based studio WeCanMake’s winning prototype, Neighbourhood Factory Futures, is a homegrown timber kit-of-parts system designed to be used for constructing low-rise apartment buildings.

With the Design Museum’s grant, the studio looks to create a neighbourhood factory model, allowing local communities to build and maintain their own homes.

WeCanMake explained it created the system as part of a wider movement aiming to make the UK a “nation of growers, producers and makers” while using reusable materials that store, rather than emit, carbon.

Prototyping PhytoFloc by social enterprise SY Ecofit in collaboration with Phyona and Studio Bio is a zero-waste project that, similarly to Local Works Studio, aims to develop plant-based insulation for building construction.

The project uses biowaste created as a byproduct of phytomining, where former industrial land is rejuvenated by plants that extract pollutants from the soil.

The project intends to recognise the value of post-industrial soils while creating a locally made, low-carbon material.

In a recent development, the grants are part of the Design Museum’s Future Observatory program, which is run in partnership with the Arts and Humanities Research Council. The winning projects were amongst 140 prototypes that were submitted to the scheme.

The museum explained that at a time when supply chains are under pressure, the Future Observatory aims to support designers’ practical research to drive the green transition.

“The climate crisis demands rapid change, and we believe that design is critically key if we are to meet that challenge,” stated Design Museum director Tim Marlow.

“The presence of Future Observatory allows us an extraordinary opportunity to get involved with practitioners and problem-solvers and have a direct impact on the development of newly introduced technologies at the frontier of current design thinking.”.

The four projects will be funded from November 2026 until July 2027. Afterwards, the prototypes will be tested and begin the commercialisation process.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every open-world game has a crowd problem. Pack the streets with people and, sooner or later, you clock the same jogger for the fifth time, and the illusion falls apart. GTA 6 breaks that wall and delivers a world filled with unique little virtual actors.

It has been revealed that having spent time in Leonida myself for my GTA 6 review, often just people-watching, eavesdropping on conversations, and spying on the game's background actors as they play out their lives, I can say this is the most alive game I've played. A regular couple rant about gentrification and other conspiracies on their apartment steps; two others argue about that latest Manatees result; two women sip coffee, gossiping about their friend's love life; one's eyes widen, brows lift, just a fraction too slowly to feel like shock.

With all I've seen, I can see why Rockstar's art team is so keen to talk about its pedestrians and background characters.

In a recent development, valmor Garcia, Senior Technical Art Director: Dynamic Art, notes Rockstar has moved on from the “monolithic” NPCs of GTAV and Red Dead Redemption 2, which were built to lower visual standards than those of the games’ main casts. The aim now is “fully fleshed-out characters with singular awareness and visual identities”, driven by dynamic moods and personalities, with their own anatomy, facial features and dialogue.

It has been revealed that garcia puts all of that on a visual par with Jason and Lucia. He also notes it’s the first time Rockstar feels it has levelled the whole cast so consistently, including world NPCs.

Recent findings suggest that valmor Garcia, Senior Technical Art Director: Dynamic Art, indicates Rockstar has moved on from the “monolithic” NPCs of GTAV and Red Dead Redemption 2, which were built to lower visual standards than those of the games’ main casts. The aim now is “fully fleshed-out characters with singular awareness and visual identities”, driven by dynamic moods and personalities, with their own anatomy, facial features and dialogue.

It has been revealed that garcia puts all of that on a visual par with Jason and Lucia. He also notes it’s the first time Rockstar feels it has levelled the whole cast so consistently, including world NPCs.

Industry observers note that mark Tennant, Vice President of Animation, conveys the scale. “There are close to a thousand animation sets for ambient activities,” he notes, “then we layer in hundreds of bespoke one-off events and custom sequences to punctuate the world and reward exploration.”.

Those everyday sets, with people hanging out and doing day-to-day jobs, “form the foundation of this living world”, according to Tennant. The variety extends to bodies, too. The team decided early to “really push the variation in character sizes and body types”, which meant building “a very robust way to share animations between characters”.

Garcia says the team built latest technology and tools “from the ground up” for the engine. The all-new in-house tech covers hair, cloth simulation and head-and-body customisation, and it’s applied across the world “to benefit all characters equally”. So the people on the street get the same tech as the leads.

It’s the little things that sell it. John Macpherson, Senior Design Director: World & Population, says that “everywhere you look, little stories constantly unfold”. That might be as simple as what someone’s wearing, how they walk and talk, or what they’re blasting from a passing car.

I see this in how characters dress and behave differently across the map. Some things are just obvious, such as characters wearing swimsuits on the beach, but Rockstar takes it further, as Leonida's beachgoers lie and chat on towels, play frisbee, and make mistakes – I snuck onto a boat party and watched as characters danced and reacted to Lucia and Jason's moves.

Most of the people you pass in Leonida will only be on screen for a moment, but Rockstar has built them as if you might stop and look; in fact, the developer wants you to stop, look and listen, and simply love being in the world. Sam Fender's People Watching is on the soundtrack for a reason.

5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

📅 19 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship.
  • It has been revealed that most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going.
  • Industry observers note that you might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

It has been revealed that most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

Industry observers note that you might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

To be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

According to recent reports, look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

“At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That mentioned, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

If someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher claims. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

Sources indicate that maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” plans fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

Recent findings suggest that “In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher says, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Recent findings suggest that instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds says. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling plans only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

Let’s say you mentioned how important it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your major day without a hint of apology.

True friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely indicates empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

According to recent reports, ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That said, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds claims. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”.

  • According to recent reports, turning 200 years old in 2027, the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society is only 50 years younger than the US as an independent country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that how do you rebrand a 200-year-old institution that wants its new logo to "feel like plants"? Plants are constantly changing; they grow, wilt, bloom, move in the wind, shed their leaves and sprout new ones. Captivating that in a permanent identity built to last years might seem like an impossible task.

According to recent reports, and yet the new identity for the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society achieves it. The logo is a clear candidate as one of the best animated logos, and the blooming rebrand also includes one of the most beautiful brand manuals I've seen. There's even a flipbook, further demonstrating the dynamism of the mark.

According to recent reports, turning 200 years old in 2027, the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society is only 50 years younger than the US as an independent country. To mark its upcoming anniversary, it brought in local design agency Smith & Diction to create an identity that better represents the breadth of what it does, from urban greening to landscaping parks and the City Harvest initiative.

In a recent development, the existing logo design was fairly generic. It could have been the identity for a financial institution – or even a retirement home, as Smith & Diction point out. Depicting a single tree, it hardly represented the rich diversity of the plant kingdom. What kind of tree was it supposed to be anyway?

According to recent reports, the agency's solution was a three-letter logo in which the letters become roots, with a different species of native plant growing from each. Smith & Diction claims the process began with the illustrations. Summer McClure drew the plants and flowers within rectangles, chosen to represent Philadelphia's grid layout of city blocks.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

The logo was then animated. Henrique Barone drew the plants growing from the letterforms, frame by frame. This allowed the creation of the flipbook (see the Instagram post below) as well as the final animation, which feels like a timelapse video from a nature documentary. A second animation was made by Justin Lawes to show the plants moving as if swaying in the breeze.

The result is a strong, versatile and dynamic logo that represents nature, the city grid, and the PHS's work to unite them.

A post shared by Smith & Diction — Design & Copywriting (@smith_diction).

It has been revealed that the logo's backed up by further custom brand illustrations based on native flora for social posts and things like menus and signs. There are also floral illustrations for sub brands, including a peony for the PHS's annual flower show.

Industry observers note that the beauty of this system is that it introduces another way in which the branding can grow like a garden. The idea is that the PHS can host workshops where people will be able to draw their own florals to fit the same dimensions, or make their own linocut prints.

The colour palette is also unconventional, again reflecting the diversity of plant life. While there's a core set of greens and blues, the palette expands to contemplate dozens of colours. As for type, Caslon Doric is the lead, backed up by the elegance of ES Park, a choice inspired by the practical simplicity of old PHS exhibition posters.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

It has been revealed that it's one of those projects that's blurs the line between brand design and art. That's apparent in the decision to produce a physical brand book, which was "designed as a reminder to touch grass and hold books".

In a recent development, "Making a shiny digital case study to talk about our partnership just felt inauthentic," Smith & Diction explains. "This isn’t a shiny digital brand, it’s rooted in the tangible: grass below your feet, warm sun on your face, the sound of birds chirping to one another from neighboring trees.".

You can purchase a copy of the book for $60 for which you also get the flip book, a lapel pin and a poster.

It has been revealed that joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when your physical set is three walls and a ceiling, whatever’s outside the window has to carry a lot of the film. For SNTIENT 2.0, the Fashion Innovation Agency’s film for London College of Fashion, that view was a bleak, abandoned city, and it lived entirely in Unreal Engine.

The story is a dystopia with a twist, set around the idea that resources have run out, humans have retreated into a simulation, and the robots left behind to look after the physical world have started to find beauty in it. “That gave us our visual starting point. A bleak, oppressive sci-fi environment with the potential for transformation,” says Dickon Knowles, director of content at Dandelion + Burdock. The finished film doesn't explore that transformation as far as originally planned, but the city still set the tone for everything else.

According to recent reports, the substantial draw of Unreal Engine 5 was speed. Working in a real-time engine meant the team could play with spaces, lighting, and textures, see the result straight away, and change it on the spot, instead of waiting for a render only to find it was wrong. “It made the whole process much more fluid,” Knowles states.

In a recent development, other routes were tried first. “We tried a couple of generative approaches to creating the city plate for the wall, but resolutions were an problem and the visual fidelity wasn’t there,” Knowles explains. “Which is why we reverted back to our existing Unreal Engine version.”.

Recent findings suggest that even then, the city needed work. The original environment was foggy and slightly desaturated, and wasn't reading through the camera as intended. Knowles reworked the fog, replacing the general wash through the scene with more detailed VDB fog, while reducing its overall presence and boosting the saturation, particularly in the city windows. The LED wall looked better with richer blacks and more contrast, which the fog had been fighting against. It needed a more vivid backdrop to work on camera.

Industry observers note that most of the city was already built before the shoot, with the team making visual refinements, grading and subtle tweaks on set. It wasn't building a digital world from scratch while the cameras were rolling. The advantage was seeing how those changes looked on the wall and through the camera, and making adjustments without waiting for a fresh render.

The city also ran on an LED wall as the view from the character’s window, which gave the performer something real to react to rather than a green screen to imagine over.

Cinematographer Ben Saffer, whose tech giant, Supervision VP, handled the virtual production, indicates the appeal was being able to capture everything together. The virtual and physical lighting could be controlled as one, so the glow on screen matched the light on set. “You’re doing it all in camera and capturing everything together at once, and you’re not having to guess at anything,” he says.

According to recent reports, the alternatives were a green screen or a pre-rendered backdrop. Knowles says cost was less of a concern than visual quality, because the city content had already been created for a previous project. “The city lights reflect on the performer’s face and on the surfaces of the props and set,” he says. “There is a level of visual immersion that is hard to capture in a studio without the LED wall to illuminate the space.”.

The LED wall wasn't simply providing something pretty to look at outside the window; it was lighting the performer and the physical set at the same time, similar to how Magnopus used Unreal Engine for Fallout. The intention was to keep post-production to a minimum, getting the footage as close to the finished shot as possible during filming.

Unreal also solved a budget problem because the film needed a shutter that rises to reveal the city, but a moving shutter built into the set wasn't realistic on the budget, and adding one in VFX would have meant losing that in-camera moment.

So the LED wall became the shutter, rising to reveal the digital city behind it. For reverse shots, a second wall on wheels could be brought in to act as a fourth wall. Because the content ran in real time, the team could swiftly render new assets for those angles, animate them, and get them moving. “It was nice to get that in camera,” Saffer says.

Sources indicate that not everything went virtual, though, as the pod itself was a physical build, because the team wanted it to feel gritty and lived-in, with the LED wall and Unreal handling the distant environment. The AI-generated dream sequence at the start was a separate part of the production, created using generative tools to show the character floating in water before she wakes up.

Recent findings suggest that the film has very few beats: the character wakes, the window opens, she looks out. Saffer notes the real challenge was getting a sense of the world and her place in it within two minutes. The team also had to make the most of the tiny space, shooting on an URSA Cine 17K 65 with prototype Atlas Lens Co. anamorphic lenses. The larger sensor meant Saffer could capture more of the set without resorting to an extreme wide-angle lens, which would have distorted the perspective.

There was still room for a bit of old-fashioned experimentation. Towards the end of the film, as the character looks towards the window, Saffer held a plastic Polly Pocket toy in front of the lens and shone his phone torch through it from the side to create an optical effect. He also played around with cling film and other materials in front of the lens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects.

UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.

“The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with upcoming spaces for art, culture and the local community,” said Waugh Thistleton Architects.

The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.

The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.

“Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room,” said the studio.

“Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character,” it continued.

“The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a newly introduced sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea.”.

Along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building’s core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings on either side of the central pavilion.

The building will be topped by a rooftop terrace, while a public toilet on the site will be renovated.

“The design draws on the proportions and character of the original building, removing later additions and reinstating lost features such as the historic belvederes which top the central tower structures,” remarked the studio.

“The beachfront facade will see a new glazing system and colonnade to each of the building’s wings, with a new sheltered archway forming a new seating terrace at the building’s heart,” it continued.

“The design seeks to reference the original architecture while providing contemporary needs of a public building. Where original features are references, these are distinguishable architecturally.”.

Emin is one of the UK’s best-known living artists. We recently produced a video of a landmark exhibition of her work at Tate Modern.

Recent projects by Waugh Thistleton Architects include prepares for the “tallest mass timber office building in the US”.

Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects.

Shigeru Ban unveils proposal for tent-like church in Rome

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.
  • The church will occupy a at the moment underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.
  • The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a at the moment underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a “fragmented urban fabric”.

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together,” said Ban.

“The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a fresh sense of belonging in the neighbourhood.”.

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci’s proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the New Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four new churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest’s residence embedded below.

According to recent reports, its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

Sources indicate that inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped blueprint, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios said will “create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities”.

Recent findings suggest that the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in New Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.

Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti’s design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry.
  • Recent findings suggest that the act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience.
  • Industry observers note that for many, tattoos are much more than art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

Recent findings suggest that the act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

Industry observers note that for many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

Industry observers note that but here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Sources indicate that getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos revealed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

Sources indicate that the relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a recent development, in a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings highlighted that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Sources indicate that keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins claims about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of massive butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

It has been revealed that two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

Sources indicate that “She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Recent findings suggest that coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins indicates change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

Sources indicate that the duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Massive Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

It has been revealed that “We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

Recent findings suggest that “The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”.

According to recent reports, humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we launched the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and said that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”.

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” said Bergh.

Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life.

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

Industry observers note that “But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”.

It has been revealed that “Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”.

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” said Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most important thing,” she continued.

Sources indicate that “Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”.

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

The hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money.

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

“The hardest thing is to earn money,” said Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”.

In a recent development, “You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”.

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” said Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”.

The duo noted funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

“All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”.

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

In a recent development, “It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” remarked Bergh. “We have aims for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”.

In a recent development, “I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Recent findings suggest that sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Recent findings suggest that many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

According to recent reports, light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing complications. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

It has been revealed that light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

According to recent reports, diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Sources indicate that regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.
